beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Hunger After All the Worlds combines a novel with an atlas of speculation.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its powerful world-makers face a problem that greater capability cannot automatically solve.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: How can imagination encounter something it has not already reduced to itself?

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book explores that tension through inhabited worlds and a revisable conceptual table.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The table classifies operations, not merely famous devices or familiar story decorations.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That approach offers readers a way to compare how invented worlds produce consequences.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Changing gravity and distributing one identity across bodies are different speculative operations.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Their importance lies in what the change makes possible or difficult.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book organizes such operations into families and combinations.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: An abundant library, for example, can make selection scarcer than information.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This method connects an imaginative premise with the social problem it creates.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It is a working grammar whose categories remain open to revision.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The novel's visits give the conceptual atlas a difficult human counterpart.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A local inhabitant does not exist merely to illustrate the visitor's theory.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The encounters preserve deadlines, relationships, and costs that a classification might flatten.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Memorial references also keep the genealogy of speculative ideas visible.
